sources.title: Karacic and colleagues, Pottery use and exchange at Saruq al-Hadid (2018)
sources.note: Institutional original metadata and abstract directly read; publisher introduction indexed, direct publisher request failed. DOI 10.1016/j.jasrep.2018.09.007, Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 22, pages 21 to 31. Temporary places integrated with sedentary settlements. The atlas geometry itself, not this research paper, supplies the public map caveats.

sources.title: Weeks and colleagues, Recent archaeological research at Saruq al-Hadid (2017)
sources.note: Direct full publisher text. Discussion on persistent places: seasonal resources and shallow water, sheep/goat herding and later camels. Do not convert alternative water mechanisms into an excavated standardized well system.

sources.title: Moore and colleagues, Bronze Age stone flaking at Saruq al-Hadid (2022)
sources.note: Direct full publisher article. Archaeological background, raw materials and reduction analysis: Horizon IV circa 1750 to 1300 BCE, bone midden, recycled cores, microlith manufacture. Specific artifact functions remain debated; technological skill is not evidence for a documented school.

sources.title: Soriano and colleagues, Goldwork technology at Saruq al-Hadid (2018)
sources.note: Indexed publisher abstract/highlights checked; direct request 403. DOI 10.1016/j.jasrep.2018.08.030. Approximately 450 gold items excavated in 2015 to 2017; lost-wax casting and deformation processes identified. Iron Age II workshop interpretation, not a claim that all inhabitants were goldsmiths.

sources.title: Ben-Yosef, Langgut and Sapir-Hen, Beyond smelting: Timna gatehouse and livestock pens (2017)
sources.note: Direct institutional full abstract, Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 11, pages 411 to 426, DOI 10.1016/j.jasrep.2016.12.010. Donkeys or mules, grape pomace and hay, dung deliberately piled at wall, probably for initial furnace heating. Timna is an adjacent regional comparison outside the imported polygon, probably early Edom, not automatically Arabic-speaking.

sources.title: Yagel and colleagues, Geochemical investigation of pre-Roman copper production at Timna (2024)
sources.note: Original article title: Pre-Roman copper industry had no polluting impact on the global environment. Exact publisher indexed full Square 16B and Conclusions text checked; direct fetch failed. Public copy uses only spatial evidence for dung/refuse disposal, not a blanket safety claim.

sources.title: Sukenik and colleagues, Plant-based dyeing of textiles from Timna (2017)
sources.note: Direct full publisher article. Introduction and Figures 2 to 5, late eleventh to tenth century BCE Site 34 textiles. Madder red and plant-based indigotin blue securely identified; woad is only probable, so public copy does not fix its species. Manufacture need not have occurred at Timna.

sources.title: Sapir-Hen and Ben-Yosef, Animal economy and metalworker status at Timna (2014)
sources.note: Direct institutional abstract, Antiquity 88, pages 775 to 790, DOI 10.1017/S0003598X00050687. Contrasts higher-value meat cuts in industrial and domestic contexts. Social rank is the authors’ interpretation, not proof that all laborers were free.

sources.title: Sapir-Hen and Ben-Yosef, Introduction of domestic camels to the southern Levant (2013)
sources.note: Institutional original abstract directly read; author-posted original PDF page 277 indexed. Tel Aviv 40, pages 277 to 285, DOI 10.1179/033443513X13753505864089. First substantial Aravah Valley occurrence no earlier than final third of tenth century BCE; not a date for the initial domestication of camels everywhere.

sources.title: ORACC RINAP: Tiglath-pileser III inscription 42, Samsi episode
sources.note: Indexed scholarly primary-text edition verified, lines 19b to 27a; direct page failed. Eighth-century BCE Assyrian royal narration, partial restorations explicitly bracketed in edition. Queen Samsi, tents, camels, tribute and Assyrian representative; hostile royal account is not a neutral census. Group with all uses of Tadmor and Yamada RINAP 1.

sources.title: OCIANA: Safaitic script and chronological scope
sources.note: Indexed original overview verified; direct request failed. Conventionally first century BCE to fourth century CE, with evidence extending beginnings to at least third century BCE. No exact date for KRS 41 or BES20 2191. Later geographical examples beyond this atlas window and outline.

sources.title: OCIANA KRS 41: a herder’s inscription at Wadi Salma
sources.note: Direct record, scholarly transliteration and translation. Passage w rʿy h- ḍʾn translated and he pastured the sheep. Public sample normalizes editorial spacing to h-ḍʾn; Roman scholarly transliteration, not modern Arabic replacement glyphs. Recorded 1989, an archaeological discovery date only.

sources.title: OCIANA BES20 2191: pasturing, older writing and longing for brothers
sources.note: Direct record edited by Josef Bloomfield and Ahmad Al-Jallad, updated 11 August 2026. Safaitic text from Wadi Miqat, Jordan; date found 2020 does not date ancient composition. Paraphrase follows edition without quoting its uncertain q<<>>{b}ll reading as a new script sample.

proposedOverrides.name: Arabian pastoral nomads
proposedOverrides.summary: Diverse pastoral communities and their regional connections, not a unified Arabian state.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Distinct contextual narrative. Exact indexed circa 1500 to 500 BCE culture. Broad repeated polygon cannot identify all inhabitants, especially settled populations; no alias association with Arabs, Arabia, Nejd or Saba.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: All three snapshots share bounds 34.764 to 59.838 E, 12.613 to 30.780 N. Point checks place Saruq al-Hadid inside, Timna Site 34 and Wadi Salma outside. Public opening and Timna section explicitly identify comparisons. The broad outline even intersects Marib; that does not turn Saba into nomads.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Two approximate exclusive phases; Saruq Horizon IV begins before map start and overlaps it. Later Safaitic writing is separated into its own later-voices section, with corpus dating distinguished from undated individual records.
batchIdentityNotes.limits: No inherited claim that all camps used camels in 1500 BCE. No invented medical remedy, toilet, school or family arrangement. Care of pack animals, camp waste organization and later familial inscriptions supply grounded everyday details.
